Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Selfee: Self-supervised Features Extraction of animal behaviors" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and K VijayRaghavan as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Mason Klein (Reviewer #1); Primoz Ravbar (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

The Reviewers agree that the paper presents a really exciting method that could have broad impact on researchers studying quantitative animal behavior. However there are some unresolved issues for establishing the credibility of the method that we would like you to address.

Essential revisions:

1) Chose one or two strong and clean datasets and take them all the way through the analysis pipeline (selfee->anomaly score->AR-HMM->DTW) instead of using different experiments for explaining different points. We suggest removing IR76b data from the story unless the experiment can be somehow justified.

2) Also show Selfee's results on a simpler data set (with Drosophila or some other animal) with single-animal video.

3) Explain the rationale behind the choice of parameters for "Selfee". Please explain why Selfee performs so poorly without the CLD component. Would a simpler architecture, with the addition of CLD, achieve similar performance as the Selfee?

4) Explore the behaviors found in different parts of the t-SNE maps and evaluate the effect of the irrelevant features on their distributions. The t-SNE maps display several clusters representing the same behaviors (Figure 2D) which suggests strong overfitting (weak generalization). The authors should at least show some examples taken from different clusters. This would illustrate why Selfee is separating behaviors that humans perceive as a single category.

5) Provide a formal comparison with one of the pre-existing methods that would in theory work on the same videos (e.g. JAABA) (Posted 6th Apr 2022).

6) Provide a supplementary table showing full genotype of all experimental animals.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall I like the paper! I will try to give as many specific, detailed comments as possible in this section.

First, to clarify some of the items I listed under "weaknesses" in the public review:

(1) Since the paper feels mainly like a Selfee methods paper, I think spending more time describing what exactly Selfee is and how it works would be appropriate. I would recommend putting an expanded version of the Methods section paragraph (lines 925-933) in the main body of the paper, briefly explaining the techniques and existing software as you go through each step. It would give a reader with little machine learning experience a better understanding of the process.

(2) Efficiency was talked about in the introduction and occasionally brought up when highlighting that Selfee doesn't need large computational/processing power to operate, but I didn't come away with a sense of how much Selfee improves on other approaches in this regard. It would be helpful to be more specific.

(3) The comparisons with DeepLabCut make sense -- if it would be straightforward to compare to other software, that might help highlight unique aspects of Selfee a bit more effectively.

(4) I don't usually recommend new experiments when I review papers, but perhaps showing Selfee's results on a simpler data set (with Drosophila or some other animal), say with single-animal video, before showing the courtship-type results, could ease a reader into the process more effectively.

(5) It would also be great, if possible, to include a small section that could operate like a guide for a novice user to try Selfee on their own data.

A few general comments:

(1) I am not a machine learning expert myself, so I hope another reviewer could evaluate Selfee's uniqueness compared to other methods, as I am taking that at face value in my review. In particular, (line 17-19), is this true that unsupervised analysis has not been used this way before?

(2) A fair amount of grammar/word usage errors, not really a problem and I assume copy editors will address? (e.g. Fast --> Quickly or Rapidly on line 15).

(3) I generally like the figures, but found Figure 2 and Figure 3 pretty difficult to read at that size. Rearranging the panels and/or using larger fonts would help readability considerably.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This work is very relevant but has some serious unresolved issues before warranting further consideration. The overall format of the paper will also have to be massively restructured to make it palatable for a wide, life-science research audience.

Major points of concern that need to be addressed:

1) In the way it is presented, the rationale behind choice of several of the parameters for "Selfee" are unclear to me. E.g.

a. Why do the live frames consist of 3 tandem frames? Is 3 somehow a special number that is easy to compute or represent as an RGB image? Why not 4 with CMYK or a higher number with a distinct colormap as is commonly done for representing depth coding.

b. The choice of AR-HMM and DTW as post-processing steps after the Selfee analysis is also a bit unclear to me. Especially because the authors do not discuss any alternatives and moreover, they don't even show great promise in the examples later in the manuscript.

2) The authors have surprisingly failed to acknowledge and cite the state of the field that directly translates to their novelty claims (Lines 56-59: "There are no pose estimation paradigms that are designed to handle multi-animal contexts"). Both multi-animal DLC (Lauer et al., 2021) and SLEAP (Perreira et al., 2020) were explicitly designed for this purpose. Not to mention a plethora tools for multi-animal behavioral classification, especially during social interactions that provide pretty much all the extracted information obtained using Selfee in this manuscript. Listing a few Drosophila specific tools:

a. JAABA (Kaabra et al., Nat Methods, 2013)

b. Matebook (Ribeiro et al., Cell 2018)

c. Flytracker (Hoopfer et al., eLife 2015)

3) The authors must provide a sup table showing full genotype of all experimental animals. Wherever possible test and controls should be in the same genetic background (this is especially true for loss of function experiments where vision and locomotion is an integral part of the behavior, like the ones done in this manuscript). Legends for videos should also be provided.

4) Figure 2 demonstrates how good Selfee is at extracting information. To do this, authors have to either look at how data clusters with respect to human annotated labels on a t-sne map or use a k-nn classification step to classify the data. Honestly, the t-sne maps in Figure 2D don't look that promising. K-nn classification looks better with around 70% F1 score. But at this point there should be a formal comparison with one of the pre-exisiting methods that would in theory work on the same videos. I suggest JAABA (or Flytracker+JAABA) since similar labels have been previously extracted using this toolkit. Same holds true for mouse data (2G-I) and especially more important because the F1 scores here are a bit low. Also panels 2F and 2I likely represent cherry picked cases where results are much better than what the scores indicate and hence are not really informative.

5) The rationale for definition of "anomaly score" (Figure 3, lines 230-249) is again poorly defended in the text. Could authors clearly define what "meta-representations of frames" means. Also, why restrict k=1 for IES? How is the +-50 frame window chosen for IAS score. Are these empirically derived values after some trial and error, or based on some priors. Since the anomaly score is quite central to the overall utility of this tool, it needs to be proposed in a much more credible way.

6) The unusual subset of neurotransmitter mutants/silenced lines used in Figure 3 data makes one wonder if the provided data is a cherry-picked subset of the full data to make the story easier. I would really appreciate if all data were shown clearly and rationally. The authors really need to establish credibility for persuading the reader to use their method.

7) Trh mutant phenotype is interesting but interpretations of secondary assays warrant some more thought. Trh neurons directly innervate Drosophila legs (Howard et al., 2019, Curr Biol.) and impact locomotion. Making a claim about social repulsion is a bit too ambitious without further segregating impact on other behaviors like walking that could impact the phenotype observed by the authors.

8) Given that the utility of AR-HMM rests on IR76b experiments which seem to be based on a false premise, it would be best if authors repeat this with one of the myriad of receptors shown to be involved in courtship. Or rather just do AR-HMM on one of the previous datasets.

9) DTW is a cool method but using increased copulation latency of blind flies to show its usability is a bit of a short-sell. It does not in any way increase the credibility of this method and I would rather suggest using DTW to look at longer scale dynamics in previous experiments (e.g. Figure 3 data), provided these are done in the correct genetic background).

Recommendation for improvement: The point of this paper is the method and not the biological findings. But the method loses credibility because there are serious problems with the way the experiments are performed and data is presented. I would recommend the authors chose one strong and clean dataset and take it all the way through their analysis pipeline (selfee->anomaly score->AR-HMM->DTW) instead of using different experiments for explaining different points. Even if the results are less interesting, if the rationale is clear and all data is shown properly this will encourage other people to try out this tool.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The figures are in a good shape, except where specifically mentioned (and assuming that the final published figures will have better resolution).

Major concerns (2):

1) Reference [9] is critically important for the understanding of how the CLD is implemented in this architecture, however, I find it difficult to access the reference. The authors should provide for an alternative. Adding more visualization of how the CLD is implemented, in Figure 2, would be helpful. The authors should compare the classification performance of Selfee with and without the CLD (for fly courtship behavior in Figure 2). This way the reader could understand the weight of the CLD in the overall architecture. Next, the authors should discuss alternative architectures with CLD and show why the SimSiam has been chosen.

2) How much of the performance of the classification (and possibly other utilities) is lost to strict end-to-end processing? The authors should show the effects of the following pre-processing steps on the t-SNE maps, the confusion matrices, and the F1 scores: a) use the raw frames instead of live-frames; b) perform simple background subtraction; c) create narrow areas of interest around the animals in each frame. Authors can add other steps such as segmentation. The prediction would be that the classification performance will improve greatly, the t-SNE maps should have fewer yet more distinct clusters, and rare behaviors should be classified better than, for example, in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 F.

claims.claim: The anomaly score of each live-frame in the query group is calculated in two steps.
claims.source: When given two groups of videos, namely the query group and the reference group, the anomaly score of each live-frame in the query group is calculated in two steps (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This describes the anomaly detection method illustrated in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The IES is defined as the k-nearest distance of the query frame against all reference frames.
claims.source: First, distances between the query live-frame and all reference live-frames are measured, and the k-nearest distance is referred to as its inter-group score (IES).
claims.evidence: This describes the first step of anomaly detection.

claims.claim: The IAS is defined as the k-nearest distance of the query frame against all other frames within its group, except those within the time window of ±50 frames.
claims.source: Therefore, an intra-group score (IAS) is introduced in the second step to eliminate these false-positive effects. We assume that those rare events should not be sampled frequently in the query groups either. Thus, the IAS is defined as the k-nearest distance of the query frame against all other frames within its group, except those within the time window of ±50 frames, because representations for frames beyond 50 frames were less similar to the current frame (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the second step of anomaly detection with supporting data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The final anomaly score is defined as the IES minus the IAS.
claims.source: The final anomaly score is defined as the IES minus the IAS.
claims.evidence: This describes the final calculation of the anomaly score.

results.result: Selfee is a self-supervised CNN that extracts comprehensive and discriminative features (Meta-representations) from animal behavior videos by training on ~5 million unlabeled frames using live-frames (three tandem frames stacked as RGB) and a SimSiam-style architecture with ResNet-50 backbone, learning invariance to augmentations while capturing both spatial and temporal information.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C21-C23, C26-C28, C33-C34, C36-C38 collectively describe the Selfee architecture and training approach. The method is well-documented with specific details about the network structure (ResNet-50 backbone, MLP projectors), training data (~5 million frames), and the live-frame preprocessing that captures temporal dynamics. The training objective and augmentation strategy are clearly specified.

results.result: Selfee features enable meaningful t-SNE visualization and classification of fly courtship behaviors, achieving 72.4% F1 score with k-NN classifier on manually annotated data, with performance comparable to human expert agreement (~70% on wing extension), and capturing fine-grained features like wing angles, distances, and spatial positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 demonstrate that Selfee extracts meaningful features through t-SNE visualization showing non-random clustering of behaviors (C39), separation based on tracking-derived features (C40-C41), and classification performance (C43) comparable to human inter-rater agreement (C45). The F1 score of 72.4% is supported by confusion matrices in Figure 3B-C.

results.result: Selfee features are comparably discriminative to FlyTracker and JAABA features for behavior classification, achieving best performance by Pearson's correlation and F1 score (Table 1), while avoiding the need for careful key point selection and feature engineering required by distance-based methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by Table 1 showing quantitative comparisons across different feature types. Selfee achieved the highest Pearson's R (0.774) and F1 score (0.629), demonstrating comparable or superior performance to engineered features. The comparison includes appropriate controls (FlyTracker with/without legs) showing the importance of feature engineering for traditional methods.

results.result: Selfee generalizes to mice mating behaviors, separating five behavior types in t-SNE visualization, with classification performance reaching 67.4% F1 score using LightGBM with temporal features, demonstrating that live-frames capture temporal information better than single frames (Table 3).
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by Figure 3D-F showing t-SNE visualization and classification results. The improvement from k-NN (59.0% F1) to LightGBM with temporal features (67.4% F1) demonstrates the value of temporal information. Table 3 provides ablation evidence that live-frames outperform single frames, validating C57-C58.

results.result: Selfee incorporates group discriminators (CLD loss) to address class imbalance and prevent mode collapse, and uses Turbo transformation to enhance color augmentations on grayscale images, with ablation studies (Table 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 5) showing these modifications improve performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by ablation studies in Table 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5. The CLD loss prevents catastrophic mode collapse (Figure 3—figure supplement 5D) and addresses the long-tail distribution of behaviors (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A). Turbo transformation improves F1 scores as shown in Table 2 comparisons.

results.result: Selfee enables frame-level anomaly detection using cosine distance between Meta-representations, with anomaly score calculated as IES minus IAS, successfully identifying ultra-fast (<0.25s) tussle behavior in CCHa2-R-RB>Kir2.1 flies that is difficult for human observers to detect.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C68 describe the anomaly detection method and its application. The method is clearly defined (C61-C64) with IES and IAS calculations. The discovery of ultra-fast tussle behavior in CCHa2-R-RB>Kir2.1 flies (C65-C67) is supported by Figure 4B-D showing significant anomaly scores and temporal dynamics. The sub-second duration (C67) makes human detection challenging, validating C68.

results.result: Selfee detected close body contact behavior in Trh knockout flies (occupying <0.15% of frames), which was validated by behavioral assays showing significantly reduced kicking rates and shorter social distances compared to controls, revealing a novel role for serotonergic neurons in social distance regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C81 present anomaly detection in Trh mutants and validation experiments. The anomaly detection (C71-C74) identified rare close-contact behaviors supported by Figure 4B, E-F. Independent validation through kicking assays (C77, Figure 4G) and social distance measurements (C78-C79, Figure 4H-J) with statistical significance (Mann-Whitney tests) confirms the biological relevance. The novelty claim (C76) is appropriately cautious ('to the best of our knowledge').

results.result: AR-HMM analysis of Selfee features successfully distinguishes control from CIS-treated mice in open field tests, identifying two behavioral modules (No.0 and No.3) with statistically significant usage differences related to distance from arena walls, consistent with previous observations of anxiety-related behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 demonstrate AR-HMM application to mice OFT data. PCA visualization (C89, Figure 5B) shows clear separation, with statistically significant differences in modules No.0 and No.3 (C90, Figure 5C with Mann-Whitney tests and multiple testing correction). The interpretation linking these modules to wall distance (C91-C93) is supported by tracking data analysis, and consistency with prior work (C92, C94) strengthens the findings.

results.result: DTW analysis of Selfee features captures long-term behavioral dynamics, successfully detecting delayed courtship in NorpA mutant flies with defective visual transduction, demonstrating that Selfee combined with DTW can identify differences in behavior latency at the video level.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 present DTW application to NorpA mutants. The prolonged courtship latency (C102) is supported by Figure 5F with statistical testing. DTW analysis (C103, Figure 5G) shows the delay as a curve below the diagonal, consistent with the latency measurement. The claim of first application to image data (C99) is appropriately cited with references to prior DTW applications to other data types.

results.result: The complete Selfee pipeline (preprocessing, feature extraction, anomaly detection, AR-HMM, and DTW) was demonstrated on mice OFT data, showing minimal false positives in anomaly detection (<0.01% of frames), consistent AR-HMM results with wall distance analysis, and DTW results matching position-based analysis, though biological significance of minor delays remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C118 describe the full pipeline demonstration. The preprocessing steps (C107-C108) are clearly documented. Anomaly detection results (C109-C111) show appropriate validation with manual inspection identifying false positives. AR-HMM (C112) and DTW (C113-C114) analyses are consistent with position-based tracking. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about biological significance (C115-C116) and need for further validation, which is scientifically appropriate rather than a weakness.

results.result: Selfee complements pose estimation methods by handling closely interacting animals where DeepLabCut, FlyTracker, and SLEAP show tracking errors, capturing global behavioral characteristics robust to occlusions, though Selfee features are less explainable than key points and benefit from animal tracking for interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C138 compare Selfee with pose estimation methods. The comparison is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing tracking errors in DeepLabCut (C130), FlyTracker (C132), and SLEAP (C133) during close interactions. The complementary nature is well-argued: Selfee handles occlusions (C136) but is less explainable (C137). The acknowledgment of limitations and complementarity (C138) is scientifically balanced.

results.result: Selfee achieves efficient training (8 hours on single RTX 3090 GPU with batch size 256) compared to typical self-supervised methods requiring 8+ GPUs, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer from mice mating to OFT (capturing CIS vs control differences) and to rat social behaviors (49.6% F1 score), enabling training-free deployment.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C149 address computational efficiency and transfer learning. Training efficiency (C140) is well-documented with specific hardware and timing. Zero-shot transfer to OFT (C143-C145) is supported by AR-HMM results in Figure 5B-D. Transfer to rat behaviors (C146-C147) achieves modest performance (49.6% F1) but demonstrates cross-species generalization. The comparison with typical self-supervised learning requirements (C139) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Selfee has three main limitations: (1) limited motion capture from 3-frame live-frames, especially for dynamic behaviors, potentially addressable with 3D convolution or spatial-temporal attention; (2) vulnerability to background textures requiring background removal in some cases; (3) potential mode-split from batch-level discrimination, addressable through fine-tuning or improved explainability via unsupervised segmentation and BagNet approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C161 honestly acknowledge limitations with supporting evidence. Limited temporal information (C150-C151) is demonstrated by better performance with temporal features in Table 3. Texture sensitivity (C153-C154) is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. Mode-split issues (C155-C156) are logical consequences of the training approach. Proposed solutions (C152, C157-C161) are appropriately speculative and cite relevant methods, showing thoughtful consideration of future improvements.

results.result: Two future directions are proposed: (1) optimizing self-supervised learning with advanced methods like DINO with ViTs for better explainability and texture robustness, or simplified instance learning for accessibility; (2) explainable behavior forecasting using representation learning with transformers to capture behavioral syntaxes beyond spatial movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C174 propose future directions with appropriate citations to relevant methods (DINO, ViTs, transformers). However, these are speculative proposals without experimental validation. The reasoning is sound—ViTs could improve texture robustness (C164), representation learning could highlight syntaxes (C172)—but these remain hypotheses. The proposals are well-motivated but cannot be evaluated as SUPPORTED without experimental evidence.

results.result: Selfee is accessible to biology laboratories, requiring only 8 hours training on a single RTX 3090 GPU, achieving 800 fps inference speed, and accepting standard top-view 2D grayscale videos without specialized equipment like depth cameras or multi-view arrays.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C178 describe practical accessibility. Training time (C175) and inference speed (C176) are specific, measurable claims supported by the methods description. Input requirements (C177) are clearly documented, and the comparison with more demanding methods (depth cameras, multi-view arrays) is appropriately cited. These practical considerations are important for method adoption and are well-supported.

results.result: The introduction establishes context by reviewing current approaches to animal behavior analysis: traditional human observation, supervised learning (limited by labels), pose estimation (less effective for direct classification, neglects some body parts, challenging for same-color animals with intensive interactions), and advantages of self-supervised learning (avoids human bias, learns invariances, produces discriminative features).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C20 provide literature review and motivation. These claims are appropriately supported by citations to relevant prior work (C7-C8, C10-C12, C15-C16, C20) or are logical inferences about method properties (C9, C17-C19). The gap identification (C2, C13) motivates the current work. The review accurately represents the state of the field based on cited literature.

results.result: Selfee was validated on three model species (flies, mice, rats) with results consistent with manual annotations and animal tracking methods, and can be validated by biological experiments. The workflow includes anomaly detection for phenotype discovery, AR-HMM for micro-dynamics and state transitions, and DTW for long-term dynamics at the video level.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25, C29-C32 describe validation strategy and workflow applications. Multi-species validation (C24) is demonstrated throughout the results. Consistency with manual annotations (C25) is shown in classification experiments. The three downstream applications (C29-C32) are clearly defined and demonstrated in subsequent results sections with appropriate citations for AR-HMM and DTW methods.

results.result: The discussion argues that Siamese CNNs with cosine similarity are well-suited for behavior analysis, enabling end-to-end training without preprocessing, and that Selfee features are meaningful and valuable, compatible with various downstream methods including classification, clustering, anomaly detection, and other unsupervised learning approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C119-C126 provide discussion and interpretation. The properties of SimSiam (C35) and Siamese CNNs (C119) are appropriately cited. The suitability of cosine similarity (C120) and end-to-end training (C121) are logical inferences supported by the experimental results. The conclusion about feature meaningfulness (C122) is justified by the validation experiments. The flexibility claims (C123-C126) are reasonable extrapolations from demonstrated applications.

results.result: Selfee is a self-supervised CNN framework that processes live-frames (stacked tandem grayscale frames) to extract discriminative Meta-representations of animal behaviors in an end-to-end manner, using a SimSiam architecture with ResNet-50 backbone and specific augmentations including Turbo transformation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers request more detailed explanation of Selfee's architecture and rationale for design choices. Reviewer 1 states 'spending more time describing what exactly Selfee is and how it works would be appropriate.' Reviewer 3 specifically requests explanation of 'why Selfee performs so poorly without the CLD component' and whether 'a simpler architecture, with the addition of CLD, achieve similar performance.' The reviewers also request clarification on the choice of 3 tandem frames for live-frames (Reviewer 2).

results.result: Selfee features achieve comparable classification performance to FlyTracker and JAABA features for fly courtship behaviors, with a mean F1 score of 72.4% using k-NN classifier, and t-SNE visualization shows that behaviors cluster in non-random patterns that correlate with human annotations and tracking-derived features.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express concerns about the t-SNE visualizations and classification performance. Reviewer 2 states 'the t-SNE maps in Figure 2D don't look that promising' and notes that 'K-nn classification looks better with around 70% F1 score. But at this point there should be a formal comparison with one of the pre-existing methods.' Reviewer 3 notes that 't-SNE maps display several clusters representing the same behaviors (Figure 2D) which suggests strong overfitting (weak generalization)' and requests examples from different clusters to explain why Selfee separates behaviors humans perceive as single categories.

results.result: For mice mating behaviors, Selfee with LightGBM classifier incorporating temporal features achieved 67.4% F1 score in classifying five behavior types including mounting, intromission, and ejaculation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 expresses concern that 'panels 2F and 2I likely represent cherry picked cases where results are much better than what the scores indicate and hence are not really informative.' The relatively low F1 score of 67.4% for mice behaviors raises questions about performance, especially given the essential revision requesting formal comparison with existing methods like JAABA.

results.result: Ablation studies show that group discriminators (CLD loss) and Turbo augmentation improve Selfee's performance, helping to prevent mode collapse and capture more useful features, and that live-frames are more discriminative than single frames for dynamic behaviors.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically requests 'compare the classification performance of Selfee with and without the CLD (for fly courtship behavior in Figure 2)' to understand 'the weight of the CLD in the overall architecture.' Reviewer 2 questions 'why do the live frames consist of 3 tandem frames?' and whether alternatives were considered. The reviewers want more systematic evaluation of design choices rather than just ablation results.

results.result: Selfee's anomaly detection method identified ultra-fast tussle behavior in CCHa2-R-RB>Kir2.1 flies lasting less than 0.25 seconds, demonstrating the ability to detect sub-second behavioral episodes that human observers tend to neglect.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'The rationale for definition of "anomaly score" (Figure 3, lines 230-249) is again poorly defended in the text' and asks for clarification on parameter choices including 'why restrict k=1 for IES? How is the +-50 frame window chosen for IAS score. Are these empirically derived values after some trial and error, or based on some priors.' Reviewer 2 also notes 'The unusual subset of neurotransmitter mutants/silenced lines used in Figure 3 data makes one wonder if the provided data is a cherry-picked subset.'

results.result: Selfee detected anomalous close body contact behavior in Trh knockout flies, which was validated by follow-up experiments showing reduced kicking rate and shorter social distances, suggesting reduced self-defensive behavior and a novel role for serotonergic neurons in social distance regulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns about interpretation: 'Trh mutant phenotype is interesting but interpretations of secondary assays warrant some more thought. Trh neurons directly innervate Drosophila legs (Howard et al., 2019, Curr Biol.) and impact locomotion. Making a claim about social repulsion is a bit too ambitious without further segregating impact on other behaviors like walking that could impact the phenotype observed by the authors.' This suggests the biological interpretation may be confounded by locomotor effects.

results.result: AR-HMM analysis of Selfee features distinguished control mice from CIS-stressed mice based on behavioral state usages, with differences related to exploratory behavior and wall-following that are consistent with previous observations of stress-induced behavioral changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the AR-HMM results for mice open field test. The findings are described as consistent with previous work (Ramirez et al., 2015), providing validation. However, Reviewer 2 suggests 'do AR-HMM on one of the previous datasets' rather than using separate datasets for different analyses.

results.result: DTW analysis of Selfee features captured prolonged courtship latency in NorpA mutant flies with defective vision, demonstrating that Selfee with DTW can detect differences in long-term behavioral dynamics such as behavior latency.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'DTW is a cool method but using increased copulation latency of blind flies to show its usability is a bit of a short-sell. It does not in any way increase the credibility of this method and I would rather suggest using DTW to look at longer scale dynamics in previous experiments (e.g. Figure 3 data).' This suggests the demonstration is not compelling enough to establish the method's utility.

results.result: Selfee complements pose estimation methods by being robust to close body contacts and occlusions during social interactions, where DeepLabCut, FlyTracker, and SLEAP show tracking errors, though Selfee features are less explainable than keypoint-based features.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 challenges the novelty claim, stating 'The authors have surprisingly failed to acknowledge and cite the state of the field that directly translates to their novelty claims (Lines 56-59: "There are no pose estimation paradigms that are designed to handle multi-animal contexts"). Both multi-animal DLC (Lauer et al., 2021) and SLEAP (Perreira et al., 2020) were explicitly designed for this purpose.' The comparison with pose estimation methods needs more rigorous evaluation.

results.result: Selfee can be trained efficiently on a single GPU in 8 hours and achieves zero-shot transfer across related datasets (mice mating to open field test, mice to rats), making it accessible for biology laboratories with ordinary desktop workstations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'I didn't come away with a sense of how much Selfee improves on other approaches in this regard. It would be helpful to be more specific' regarding efficiency claims. Reviewer 2 questions whether the zero-shot transfer results (F1 score of 49.6% for rats) are sufficient to demonstrate practical utility. The accessibility claims need more concrete comparisons with existing methods.

results.result: The complete Selfee pipeline (feature extraction, anomaly detection, AR-HMM, DTW) was demonstrated on mice open field test data, showing minimal false positives in anomaly detection and consistency between Selfee embeddings and position-based analyses.
results.evaluation: This result addresses the essential revision requesting 'one or two strong and clean datasets and take them all the way through the analysis pipeline (selfee->anomaly score->AR-HMM->DTW) instead of using different experiments for explaining different points.' However, reviewers note concerns about biological significance of some findings and request removal of weaker datasets (IR76b) unless justified.

results.result: Selfee has limitations including limited temporal information capture from 3-frame live-frames, vulnerability to background textures, and potential mode-split issues where minor irrelevant differences are amplified, though these could be addressed with future improvements.
results.evaluation: These limitations are acknowledged by the authors and not disputed by reviewers. Reviewer 3 specifically requests evaluation of 'effects of the following pre-processing steps on the t-SNE maps, the confusion matrices, and the F1 scores: a) use the raw frames instead of live-frames; b) perform simple background subtraction; c) create narrow areas of interest around the animals' to understand the cost of end-to-end processing.

comparisons.comparison: Both address Selfee architecture (C3, C21-C23, C26-C28, C33-C34, C36-C38). OpenEval finds the method well-documented and SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers find it UNCERTAIN, requesting more detailed explanation of design choices, rationale for architecture decisions, and clarification on specific parameters like the choice of 3 tandem frames.

Both evaluate feature extraction and classification performance (C39-C45). OpenEval finds t-SNE clustering and F1 scores (72.4%) SUPPORTED and comparable to human agreement. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, noting t-SNE maps 'don't look that promising,' expressing concerns about multiple clusters for same behaviors suggesting overfitting, and requesting formal comparison with existing methods.

Both address performance comparisons (C46-C49). OpenEval finds quantitative comparisons in Table 1 SUPPORTED, showing Selfee's superior performance. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY about the same results, noting concerns about cherry-picked visualizations and requesting formal comparison with methods like JAABA.

Both evaluate temporal features and classification (C50-C52). OpenEval finds the improvement from k-NN to LightGBM SUPPORTED by Figure 3D-F. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, suggesting panels may represent cherry-picked cases and questioning whether results are truly informative given relatively low F1 scores.

Both address live-frame ablation (C57-C58). OpenEval finds Table 3 ablation evidence SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, specifically questioning why 3 tandem frames were chosen and whether alternatives were systematically evaluated.

Both evaluate CLD loss and design choices (C53-C56). OpenEval finds ablation studies SUPPORTED showing CLD prevents mode collapse. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, requesting comparison of classification performance with/without CLD specifically for fly courtship and questioning the weight of CLD in overall architecture.

Both address anomaly detection method and ultra-fast tussle discovery (C59-C68). OpenEval finds the method clearly defined and discovery SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, stating the rationale is 'poorly defended,' questioning parameter choices (k=1 for IES, ±50 frame window), and wondering if data represents cherry-picked subset of mutants.

Both evaluate Trh mutant anomaly detection and validation (C69-C81). OpenEval finds the discovery and validation experiments SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical testing. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, raising concerns that Trh neurons directly innervate legs and impact locomotion, suggesting claims about social repulsion may be confounded by locomotor effects.

Both address AR-HMM application to mice OFT (C89-C95). OpenEval finds clear separation and statistical significance SUPPORTED, consistent with prior work. Peer reviewers also find this SUPPORTED without specific concerns, though suggest applying AR-HMM to previous datasets rather than using separate datasets for different analyses.

Both evaluate DTW application to NorpA mutants (C99-C105). OpenEval finds the prolonged courtship latency and DTW analysis SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, stating the demonstration is 'a bit of a short-sell' and suggesting DTW should be applied to longer-scale dynamics in previous experiments to better establish utility.

Both address full pipeline demonstration (C106-C118). OpenEval finds preprocessing, anomaly detection, AR-HMM, and DTW analyses SUPPORTED, noting appropriate acknowledgment of uncertainty. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, requesting one or two strong datasets taken through the entire pipeline rather than different experiments for different points, and suggesting removal of weaker datasets like IR76b.

Both evaluate comparison with pose estimation methods (C127-C138). OpenEval finds the comparison SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment of complementarity. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, challenging novelty claims and noting failure to acknowledge that multi-animal DLC and SLEAP were explicitly designed for multi-animal contexts, requiring more rigorous evaluation.

Both address computational efficiency and transfer learning (C139-C149, C175-C178). OpenEval finds training efficiency and zero-shot transfer SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN, stating they didn't get a sense of how much Selfee improves on other approaches and questioning whether F1 score of 49.6% for rats demonstrates practical utility, requesting more concrete comparisons.

Both address limitations (C150-C156). OpenEval finds honest acknowledgment of limitations SUPPORTED with supporting evidence. Peer reviewers also find these SUPPORTED without dispute, and specifically request evaluation of preprocessing steps' effects on performance to understand the cost of end-to-end processing.

OpenEval evaluates future directions (C162-C174) as UNCERTAIN since they are speculative proposals without experimental validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific future direction claims.

OpenEval finds practical accessibility claims (C175-C178) SUPPORTED with specific metrics. Peer reviewers partially overlap with R10, expressing UNCERTAINTY about efficiency claims and requesting more specific comparisons with other approaches.

OpenEval finds literature review and motivation (C1-C2, C7-C20) SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No direct corresponding peer review evaluation, though peer R9 challenges some novelty claims related to this background.
OpenEval finds validation strategy and workflow applications (C24-C25, C29-C32) SUPPORTED. No direct corresponding peer review evaluation of these methodological overview claims.

OpenEval finds discussion and interpretation (C35, C119-C126) SUPPORTED with appropriate reasoning. Peer R1 shares only C35, focusing on architecture explanation requests rather than these interpretive claims.
